questions.explain: CommandBehavior.SequentialAccess streams large NVARCHAR/VECTOR columns without buffering the whole row; combined with yield/IAsyncEnumerable, memory stays flat regardless of result size and generation can start early.
options: Load everything into a DataTable first
CommandBehavior.SequentialAccess with IAsyncEnumerable/yield — stream rows into the prompt builder without buffering
questions.q: How should large retrieval result sets be read on the chat path?

questions.explain: Buffer ~50 tokens or 2 seconds, then UPDATE the in-progress message row — crash recovery replays from the last flush; one INSERT per token is absurd and one INSERT at the end loses everything on crash.
options: Buffer tokens and flush periodically (e.g., 50 tokens or 2 seconds) via UPDATE of the in-progress row
One INSERT at the end only
questions.q: What is the middle path for persisting streaming tokens?

questions.explain: Three defenses: server-sent heartbeats every 15s for idle connections, command timeouts with resume-from-last-flush, and an orphan-stream reaper marking streams dead after 10 minutes without a flush as abandoned with a regenerate affordance.
options: Restart the server on any failure
Heartbeats for idle connections, timeouts with resume-from-flush, and an orphan-stream reaper for dead streams
questions.q: How are broken streams defended against?

questions.explain: Unbounded server-side buffering for slow clients is a memory leak — use bounded channels (e.g., capacity 200) so the reader pauses when full, and stop generation entirely when the client disconnects; tokens burned for nobody are pure waste.
options: Apply backpressure with bounded channels and stop generating when the client disconnects
questions.q: What is backpressure and why does it matter for streaming?

questions.explain: Log stream lifecycle events — started, first-token latency, flush count, completion or abandonment reason — into the audit tables; only per-stream telemetry distinguishes 'model is slow' from 'network is slow' from 'client went away.'
options: Log stream lifecycle events (started, first-token latency, flushes, completion/abandonment) to distinguish model vs network vs client problems
